#### ! Scenario

*Or what to do when your dependency graph turns into a cycle*
This scenario demonstrates how sbt handles a cycle between external libraries, and how differently it treats a cycle between its own sub-projects.

::: {.callout-note title="Tool Versions"}
This scenario was tested with **sbt 1.12**, which uses the **Coursier** resolver (the default since sbt 1.3). On sbt 1.x the older Ivy engine can still be selected with `useCoursier := false`; under Ivy, resolution edge cases differ and Ivy-only settings such as `conflictManager` apply (Coursier ignores them). `dependencyTree` is built in since **sbt 1.4**; earlier versions need the sbt-dependency-graph plugin. sbt 2.0 (June 2026) keeps these resolution rules, removes the Ivy opt-out, adds native BOM import, and turns Test-configuration eviction warnings into errors; the demos here target sbt 1.x.
:::

#### ! Example

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 4.4
graph LR
    Root[Project Root] --> LibA[lib-circle-a:1.0.0]
    LibA --> LibB[lib-circle-b:1.0.0]
    LibB --> LibA
```

```{.scala include="build.sbt" snippet="s10-deps"}
```

#### ! Expect
"This should fail. A depends on B, and B depends on A. It's an infinite loop."

#### ! Actual
Both `lib-circle-a:1.0.0` and `lib-circle-b:1.0.0` resolve and the build succeeds. Coursier notices it has already visited `lib-circle-a`, stops recursing, and says nothing about it.

#### ! Why
A cycle between *external* artifacts is legal for the JVM: classes in two JARs can reference each other freely, because the classpath is flat. Resolvers tolerate it to support legacy libraries that were split badly, and they break the cycle silently; there is no warning, no eviction entry, nothing in `sbt evicted`. A cycle between *sub-projects* in a multi-project build is different: sbt must order project loading and compilation, so it refuses with a "cyclic reference" error.

#### ! Fix
There is nothing to fix at the build level; resolution works. If the cycle is in code you own, extract the shared types into a third module that both depend on, which removes the cycle at the design level. If it is in a third-party library, note it and move on.

#### ! Risk
* LOW Consuming two third-party artifacts that reference each other; the JVM does not care.
* MEDIUM Treating the silence as proof that the graph is healthy; cycles usually mean one artifact was split without a clean boundary.
* HIGH Introducing a cycle between your own sub-projects and discovering it as a build-load failure after a large refactor.

#### ! Control
Run `sbt dependencyTree` after adding a dependency and look for an artifact that appears beneath itself. Keep sub-project dependencies acyclic by design; sbt will enforce it for you, but late.

#### ! Check
**Fast check:** `sbt dependencyTree`

**What to look for:** `lib-circle-b` beneath `lib-circle-a` with no further expansion, and no warning anywhere in the output.

**Conclusion:** sbt resolves external cycles silently and forbids project cycles outright.

#### ! Scales
Circular dependencies are a design smell. In the Scala ecosystem they sometimes arise when library authors split a project into `api` and `impl` modules and accidentally create cross-dependencies. The fix is to extract shared types into a third, independent module.

#### ! Takeaway
sbt tolerates cycles between external libraries silently, and forbids them between sub-projects.

*   [MS10](../../maven-demo/scenario-10-circular/guide.qmd) / [GS10](../../gradle-demo/scenario-10-circular/guide.qmd) - The same cycle in Maven and Gradle: external cycles silent, project cycles fatal, in all three.

#### ! Wild

The project-level version of this failure is familiar to anyone who has grown an sbt build: `lazy val core = project.dependsOn(util)` and, months later, someone adds `lazy val util = project.dependsOn(core)` to reach a helper. sbt refuses to load the build with a cyclic-reference error, which is the better outcome. The external version never announces itself, which is why a cycle between two third-party JARs can sit in a production classpath for years without anyone noticing.
